input.rationale: The open gap asks whether the off-main-thread execution of the fast path ever produces a harmful outcome. Rather than hunt for a race window that may not be winnable, this turn targets a facet of the same handler that is deterministic and that the earlier reasoning walked past: processHeartbeat checks the node's shutdown channel first and returns without responding when it is closed, while the transport that dispatched the request waits for a response on the channel it supplied. The state that exposes it is ordinary - a caller that shuts the node down without waiting on the shutdown future leaves the transport open, and the node's own shutdown future is what closes it. So the harness builds the same single node over the same fast-path transport, delivers one heartbeat while the node is live as a control, then shuts the node down without closing the transport and delivers another heartbeat with a term one above the node's current term, recording whether a response ever arrives inside a bounded interval and whether the term moved. The term operand is what makes the outcome interpretable rather than merely timed: if the handler returned at its shutdown check, no term logic ran and the term stays put, whereas a response plus a term change would mean the handler ran normally and the suspicion is defeated. I record the question as a gap on the same investigation rather than as a new one, and I do not assert anything about the outcome until the receipt exists.

gaps.question: When a heartbeat is delivered on the transport fast path while the Raft node is shut down but its transport is still open, does the caller ever receive a response, and does the handler's shutdown check prevent the term logic from running?

scope.description: On one real single-node Raft instance built over a transport that implements the heartbeat fast path, deliver one empty heartbeat while the node is live as a control, then shut the node down while leaving its transport open and deliver a second empty heartbeat, emitting one CA_EVENT JSON line that records whether each delivery got a response, how long the second waited, and the node's term and state around each.
assumptions: The wrapper transport reproduces the network transport's classification, synchronous dispatch to the installed handler and response wait faithfully, so the handler under test is the production processHeartbeat and the appendEntries it calls.

Calling Shutdown() without waiting on the returned future leaves the in-memory transport open, which is the state a caller creates when it does not wait, and the transport is only closed when the shutdown future is waited on at the end of the test.

The second heartbeat carries a term one above the node's current term, so if the handler ran its term logic the term would move and be observable; a term that stays put together with no response is evidence the handler returned at its shutdown check.

A bounded response wait is the only practical way to observe a missing response in-process; the zero-response reading is interpreted together with the source fact that the handler has no other response path once the shutdown channel is closed.

experiment.prefix: The harness (draft/assurance_generated_test.go) is one TestAssurance-prefixed test in the captured package plus a local transport wrapper. It creates a real in-memory transport, wraps it in a type that stores the handler set by NewRaft and dispatches strictly empty AppendEntries requests to it on the caller's goroutine before waiting on the supplied response channel, bootstraps a single-voter configuration with BootstrapCluster and starts the node with NewRaft over in-memory stores, snapshots and MockFSM, then waits (bounded) for Leader state. It records the term, delivers an empty heartbeat one term above it through the wrapper's fast path with a bounded wait and records the control outcome, term and state. It then calls Shutdown() and deliberately does not wait on the returned future, sleeps briefly so the node's routines observe the shutdown, records the term and state, and delivers a second empty heartbeat one term above the current one with a bounded wait, recording whether a response arrived, how long the wait was and whether the term moved. It prints one CA_EVENT JSON line with all of these operands and only then waits on the shutdown future, which is what closes the transport.

investigations.question: For a running cluster, does the public configuration API expose the index of the latest configuration entry, and what value does a caller actually receive from ConfigurationFuture.Index()?
investigations.hypothesis: GetConfiguration() constructs configurationsFuture{latest: r.getLatestConfiguration()} and responds immediately, so latestIndex/committedIndex stay zero and Index() returns 0 for every call, independent of cluster state; the real r.configurations.latestIndex is transferred to callers only through configurationsCh. Stats() publishes the same zero as latest_configuration_index, so the reported configuration index is a constant while the reported configuration itself is live. Confirmed by observation on a running bootstrapped leader: main-thread latest index 1 versus public index 0 in one execution.
investigations.discriminator: On one running bootstrapped leader, sample f.Index() and Stats()["latest_configuration_index"] together with the main-thread latestIndex obtained from the same instance over configurationsCh; if the public values track the real index the hypothesis is wrong, if the public values stay 0 while the main-thread index is >= 1 it holds. Executed: the public values stayed 0 while the main-thread index was 1.

knowledge.assertion: GetConfiguration() carries only the Configuration (latestIndex left zero), so ConfigurationFuture.Index() is 0 on every call while the main thread holds the real latest configuration index and releases it only over configurationsCh
Stats() publishes latest_configuration_index from the same GetConfiguration() future, i.e. the constant string "0", next to a live latest_configuration
nextConfiguration enforces the caller's precondition only when prevIndex > 0, so the 0 that the public API returns disables the configuration compare-and-swap the API documents

investigations.question: When authority over a node is lost by Shutdown() rather than by stepping down, does an already-accepted Apply/Barrier duty (a logFuture sitting in the buffered applyCh) still have a completion path?
investigations.hypothesis: Apply and Barrier hand the caller a logFuture as soon as the send into applyCh succeeds; with BatchApplyCh the channel is buffered, so acceptance and consumption are separate events. That logFuture has no ShutdownCh, Shutdown() closes shutdownCh and sets state Shutdown without draining applyCh, and both the main loop and runFSM leave on shutdownCh, so a future left in the buffer has no producer that can respond it: Error() blocks indefinitely and the caller's timeout, which only guarded the enqueue, cannot save it. runLeader's defer responds only futures on leaderState.inflight, so it does not cover a future that was never dispatched. Confirmed by observation: accepted in state Leader, still queued and unresponded after state Shutdown.
investigations.discriminator: Occupy the main loop inside a handler (a public Restore with a caller-supplied reader that stalls on its first Read, which is the handshake), accept one Barrier future through the ordinary public path so it lands in the buffered applyCh, then call Shutdown() and observe whether the future is ever responded: a completion would defeat the suspicion and must name the responding producer, while non-completion together with the future still being queued in applyCh shows the duty was accepted and then lost. Executed: no completion; the duty stayed queued with the node in state Shutdown.

knowledge.assertion: the caller's timeout guards only the enqueue, and the returned logFuture has no ShutdownCh, so completion is unbounded once the duty is accepted
Shutdown() drains nothing and runLeader's defer covers only leaderState.inflight, so a duty left in applyCh loses its producer

investigations.question: When a caller names a server that holds no vote as the target of an explicit leadership transfer, does the named server acquire leadership, and what happens to the sitting leader's authority?
investigations.hypothesis: LeadershipTransferToServer forwards the caller's id and address to the transfer routine, which only requires a replication state for that server, so a vote-less member is accepted as a target. On that target the TimeoutNow handler sets Candidate and the leadership-transfer flag unconditionally and the candidate loop skips pre-vote because of that flag, so the target runs a real election at term+1; but electSelf casts a self-vote only when the local server is a Voter in the latest configuration, and voters receiving a RequestVote from a member that holds no vote reject it - after already adopting the higher term. The requested transfer is therefore unachievable: the named target can never win, while its higher-term vote request deposes the sitting leader, and the caller's future is answered without error because losing leadership during a transfer is reported as success. Observed twice, on separate clusters with the same harness: target_ever_leader=false, transfer_err empty, term 2 to 4, original leader back in Leader state, and in both runs the target's term-3 campaign skipped pre-vote while the recovery election at term 4 ran one.
investigations.discriminator: Demote one real follower to a non-voter through the public API, then call LeadershipTransferToServer on that member and sample the real nodes for a bounded interval: whether the named target ever reaches Leader, which servers do lead, whether the original leader still leads at the end, the reported transfer error, and the term before and after. Executed twice with identical operands (CheckRuns 2b61659461634c04b53ec61c35541227 and cfde738278f04108b377b912cb3eb339); the control with a voter target (7224dba1ed234879b0cb1c65e5161bf7) moved leadership to the named server with a single term step.

investigations.question: Does the documented staging phase of AddVoter exist in the implementation: can a server added through the public AddVoter API be a Nonvoter or Staging member that the leader later promotes once it has caught up?
investigations.hypothesis: The public documentation for AddVoter states that the server is added as a staging server and that the leader promotes it to a voter once it is ready, and the membership design notes list catching new servers up before granting them a vote as a main goal. The implementation does not have that phase: nextConfiguration builds the AddVoter entry with Suffrage Voter outright, the separate Staging suffrage is only reachable by an explicit Promote command, and the library's own command documentation says AddStaging was actually AddVoter and is deprecated in its favour. The in-tree unit expectations agree with the implementation, expecting a Voter for a member added through AddVoter from missing, Staging or Nonvoter states, so the state the documentation describes is never entered through the public API and the promotion duty it describes is owed by nobody.
investigations.discriminator: Trace every producer of a configuration entry for AddVoter and every consumer of the Staging suffrage: if the only public path that can add a member writes Suffrage Voter and nothing in the non-test code ever issues Promote, the documented staging phase and its promotion duty do not exist, and the mismatch is decidable by reading rather than by execution. Executed by reading: the AddVoter case writes Voter, Promote is only reached by an explicit Promote command that no non-test caller issues, and the unit expectations for AddVoter match the AddStaging cases. An end-to-end witness is queued to confirm the consequence that the added member votes immediately.

knowledge.assertion: nextConfiguration's AddVoter case writes Suffrage Voter into the very entry that adds the member, so no Staging state is entered on that path and the promotion duty the doc describes is owed by nobody

investigations.question: Does the transport heartbeat fast path run appendEntries outside the main thread, and can that be observed as a term or leader-state change while the main loop is provably occupied?
investigations.hypothesis: raft.go marks processHeartbeat and appendEntries as main-thread-only, yet api.go installs processHeartbeat as the transport's heartbeat handler; the network transport classifies a strictly empty AppendEntries request (no previous entry, no entries, no leader commit index) as a heartbeat and dispatches it from its connection goroutine. That request still runs appendEntries' term logic before anything about entries matters, so an empty heartbeat carrying a term above the node's current term calls setState(Follower) and setCurrentTerm from that goroutine, mutating state the rest of the package treats as owned by the main thread. The in-memory transport used by the test facility explicitly does not support the handler, so the path is unreachable in the harness shapes used so far; a wrapper transport that installs the handler and fast-paths empty heartbeats the way the network transport does removes that obstacle without touching production code.
investigations.discriminator: Use a transport that implements the fast path the way the network transport does - forwarding strictly empty AppendEntries requests to the installed handler on the caller's goroutine - occupy the main loop deterministically with the already-validated Restore stall handshake, then deliver one empty heartbeat whose term is above the node's current term and read the node's term and leader state while the main loop is still inside its handler. A term or leader-state change observed inside that window witnesses off-main-thread mutation; no change, or a change only after the loop resumes, would defeat the suspicion. Queued for execution with exactly that harness.

scope.description: Read, from one running bootstrapped three-node cluster, the public configuration index (GetConfiguration().Index(), Stats()["latest_configuration_index"]) and the main-thread latestIndex/committedIndex of the same node, and emit them as one CA_EVENT JSON line.
assumptions: MakeCluster(3, t, nil) performs a real bootstrap, so the cluster has a real configuration entry at index 1 and a genuinely elected leader.
The configurationsCh request is the same producer path snapshot.go uses to obtain the committed configuration index, so it reads the main thread's authoritative values rather than a supplied premise.
The one committed Apply is only there to move applied/commit indexes past the configuration entry so that the sampled state is unambiguous.

basis.prefix: The harness (draft/assurance_generated_test.go) is a single TestAssurance-prefixed test in the captured package. Initialization is the package's own test facility: MakeCluster(3, t, nil) with no injected Config, which bootstraps and elects a leader from real instances in one process; c.Leader() fails the test unless exactly one node is in Leader state. The test then commits one client command through the public Apply API so applied_index and commit_index are past the bootstrapped configuration entry, sends a real configurationsFuture to the leader's configurationsCh (setting ShutdownCh so the request cannot hang) to read the main thread's latestIndex/committedIndex and server count, calls the public GetConfiguration() and Stats() on that same instance, and prints one CA_EVENT JSON line containing the leader address, both indexes from the main thread, the public index, both server counts, and the Stats strings, so the comparison is between independently produced values on one node.

scope.description: On one real bootstrapped cluster, accept a Barrier future while the main loop is occupied by a public Restore whose caller-supplied reader stalls, then call Shutdown() and emit one CA_EVENT JSON line recording whether the accepted future ever completed, how many duties remained queued in applyCh, the channel capacity, and the node state before acceptance and after shutdown.
assumptions: MakeCluster(3, conf) with conf.BatchApplyCh = true is a supported public configuration; BatchApplyCh buffers applyCh to MaxAppendEntries (config.go:169-174), which is what allows acceptance without a consumer.

Occupying the main loop with Restore and a reader that blocks on its first Read models a caller-supplied backup stream that stalls; the reader's first Read is the handshake proving the loop is inside that handler and can no longer select on applyCh.
The control Barrier on the undisturbed leader establishes that the same call does complete while a producer is available, so a later non-completion is not the call being unusable in this harness.
The reader is released after sampling so the occupied handler can return and the node can shut down cleanly; the release happens after the observation and cannot affect it.

basis.prefix: The harness (draft/assurance_generated_test.go) is one TestAssurance-prefixed test in the captured package. It builds a real three-node cluster with MakeCluster(3, t, inmemConfig(t)) after setting BatchApplyCh = true and takes the single elected leader via c.Leader(). First it runs the control: leader.Barrier(0).Error() on the undisturbed leader, recorded as control_barrier_err. Then it occupies the main loop through the public API by calling leader.Restore(&SnapshotMeta{Version:1, Index:1, Term:1, Size:1}, reader, 0) in a goroutine, where reader is a caller-supplied io.Reader whose first Read closes a started channel and then blocks until released; receiving on started is the freeze handshake. While the loop is inside that handler the test accepts the duty through the ordinary public path by calling leader.Barrier(0) in a goroutine and taking the returned future, recording the node state at acceptance. It then calls leader.Shutdown() without waiting on the shutdown future and, for a bounded interval, watches whether duty.Error() ever returns, recording result as no_completion or completed:<err> plus waited_ms; it samples len(leader.applyCh) and cap(leader.applyCh) and the node state afterwards, which shows whether the accepted duty is still sitting in the buffer with no consumer. Finally it releases the reader, records the error the Restore call returns once the handler resumes, and prints one CA_EVENT JSON line with all of these operands, so the decisive facts are the completion result, the queue depth, and the two node states observed on one instance in one execution.

scope.description: On one real four-node cluster, demote one follower to a non-voter through the public API, name it as the target of an explicit leadership transfer, and emit one CA_EVENT JSON line recording the reported transfer error, whether the named target ever reached Leader, which servers led during a bounded interval, the state of the original leader and of the target at the end, and the cluster term before and after.
assumptions: MakeCluster(4, t, nil) gives four real voters and a real leader; DemoteVoter is supported at protocol version 3, so the target stays a connected, log-receiving member of the committed configuration that simply holds no vote.
The target is chosen among nodes actually in Follower state, so it is a viable replication peer and the transfer routine's catch-up wait can be satisfied and the TimeoutNow actually delivered.
The bounded 3 s sampling window only observes leadership outcomes; the claim that a vote-less member cannot win rests on the election code (self-vote and voter gate), not on the window length.

basis.prefix: The harness (draft/assurance_generated_test.go) is one TestAssurance-prefixed test in the captured package. It bootstraps a real four-voter cluster with MakeCluster(4, t, nil), takes the single elected leader via c.Leader(), waits for a follower using c.WaitEvent and c.GetInState, and demotes that follower with leader.DemoteVoter(target.localID, 0, 5s), recording demote_err and confirming the target's suffrage from the leader's latest configuration. It samples the maximum current term across c.rafts, then calls leader.LeadershipTransferToServer(target.localID, target.localAddr) through the public API and records the error its future reports. It then polls every 20 ms for up to 3 s across all nodes in c.rafts, recording every address observed in Leader state, whether the named target was ever among them, and whether the original leader led again, and finally records the maximum term after the window and the end states of the original leader and the target. All operands are printed in one CA_EVENT JSON line, so the decisive facts (reported transfer outcome, who led, whether the named target ever led, term movement) come from the same nodes in one execution.

scope.description: Control case on the same explicit leadership-transfer path: on a real four-node cluster, name a server that still holds its vote as the transfer target and emit one CA_EVENT JSON line recording the reported transfer error, whether the named target ever reached Leader, which servers led during a bounded interval, the end states of the original leader and the target, and the term before and after.
assumptions: MakeCluster(4, t, nil) with no demotion is the same cluster shape as the vote-less case, so the configuration, the catch-up wait and the TimeoutNow delivery are unchanged and only the target's suffrage differs.
The target is again chosen from nodes in Follower state, so it is a viable replication peer and the transfer routine's catch-up wait can be satisfied.

The control is a same-cause case, not a requirement check: it separates 'transfer works in this harness' from 'a vote-less target cannot take leadership', and its outcome does not by itself settle the attribution of the earlier term movement.

basis.prefix: The harness (draft/assurance_generated_test.go) is one TestAssurance-prefixed test in the captured package, identical to the vote-less-target case except that the target is never demoted. It bootstraps a real four-voter cluster with MakeCluster(4, t, nil), takes the single elected leader via c.Leader(), waits for a follower using c.WaitEvent and c.GetInState, confirms from the leader's latest configuration that the target's suffrage is Voter, samples the maximum current term across c.rafts, calls leader.LeadershipTransferToServer(target.localID, target.localAddr) through the public API and records the error its future reports, then polls every 20 ms for up to 3 s across all nodes in c.rafts recording every address observed in Leader state, whether the named target was ever among them, and whether the original leader led again. It finishes by recording the maximum term after the window and the end states of the original leader and the target, and prints one CA_EVENT line tagged transfer_to_voter so the control event is distinguishable from the vote-less-target event in the same investigation.

scope.description: End-to-end witness on one real cluster: join a fresh, empty node through the public AddVoter API, record the suffrage the leader wrote for that member and the suffrage the new node itself sees, then take one original voter away and record whether a new command still commits - which it can only if the freshly added member counts as a voter.
assumptions: MakeCluster(2) plus MakeClusterNoBootstrap(1) merged and fully connected is the in-tree way to join a fresh node (raft_test.go:258-279), and the join itself is the public AddVoter call made by the elected leader.

Disconnecting one original voter is the discriminator: with three voters and one disconnected, a majority needs exactly the remaining original voter plus the new member, so a commit is only reachable if the new member votes; if the new member were the non-voting member the documentation describes, no majority would be reachable.
The apply future is waited on under a bounded interval because the completion of an accepted apply is not bounded by the caller's timeout.

basis.prefix: The harness (draft/assurance_generated_test.go) is one TestAssurance-prefixed test in the captured package. It bootstraps a real two-node cluster with MakeCluster(2, t, nil) and keeps a copy of the original members, creates a fresh single-node cluster with MakeClusterNoBootstrap(1, t, nil), merges the two clusters and fully connects them, then takes the elected leader with c.Leader() and the fresh node as the join target, identifying the other original voter as the peer to remove later. The join is the public leader.AddVoter(newNode.localID, newNode.localAddr, 0, 5s); its future is waited on under a bounded interval, recording add_err and, when it returned, the entry index it reports. The test then records the suffrage of the new member in the leader's latest configuration and in the new node's own latest configuration, and counts the voters in that configuration. It calls c.Disconnect on the other original voter's address and then applies one command through the public API, waiting on the apply future under a bounded interval and recording apply_with_one_original_voter_gone as committed, an error, or no_completion. Finally it records the new node's last index, the leader's state, and prints one CA_EVENT JSON line with all of these operands, so the decisive facts (the suffrage written for the added member, and whether a command can still commit with one original voter gone) come from the same cluster in one execution.

scope.description: On one real single-node Raft instance built over a transport that implements the heartbeat fast path, occupy the main loop inside a handler, deliver one empty heartbeat with a term above the node's current term, and emit one CA_EVENT JSON line recording the term and leader state sampled while the loop is still blocked, together with the heartbeat response and the states after the loop resumes.
assumptions: The wrapper transport reproduces the network transport's classification and dispatch faithfully (term set, leader address present, zero previous entry and term, no entries, zero leader commit index) and installs the handler exactly as NewRaft expects, so the handler under test is the production processHeartbeat and the appendEntries it calls.

The freeze handshake used here is the one already validated elsewhere in this run: the caller-supplied reader's first Read proves the main loop is inside its handler, so any term or state read before releasing it cannot have been produced by the main loop.
One node bootstrapped as the only voter becomes leader on its own, so no peer traffic interferes with the sample.
A term and state change in that window is a behaviour of the fast path; whether it has a harmful consequence is a separate question, and this execution does not claim one.

basis.prefix: The harness (draft/assurance_generated_test.go) is one TestAssurance-prefixed test in the captured package plus two helper types it defines locally. It creates a real in-memory transport, wraps it in fastPathTransport, sets the config's LocalID to that address, bootstraps a single-voter configuration with BootstrapCluster and starts the node with NewRaft using an in-memory store, snapshot store and MockFSM, then waits (bounded) for the node to reach Leader state. It occupies the main loop by calling the public Restore with a caller-supplied reader whose first Read closes a channel and then blocks; receiving on that channel is the freeze handshake. While the loop is blocked it samples the node's term and state, builds an empty AppendEntriesRequest with a leader address and a term one above the current term, and delivers it through fastPathTransport.deliverHeartbeat, which applies the network transport's classification and invokes the installed handler on this goroutine, recording the returned success flag or error. It then samples the term and state again while the loop is still blocked, releases the reader so the occupied handler can return, records the Restore error and the states after release, prints one CA_EVENT JSON line with all operands, and shuts the node down.

result.summary: The open gap asks whether the off-main-thread fast path ever produces a harmful outcome. Rather than hunt for a race window that may not be winnable, this turn targets a facet of the same handler that is deterministic and that my earlier reasoning walked past: processHeartbeat checks the node's shutdown channel first and returns without responding when it is closed, while the transport that dispatched the request waits on the response channel it supplied. The state that exposes this is ordinary rather than exotic - a caller that shuts the node down without waiting on the shutdown future leaves the transport open, and it is the node's own shutdown future that closes it. So the new harness builds the same single node over the same fast-path transport, delivers one heartbeat while the node is live as a control, then shuts the node down without closing the transport and delivers a second heartbeat one term above the node's current term, recording whether a response ever arrives inside a bounded interval and whether the term moved. That term operand is what makes the outcome interpretable rather than merely timed: if the handler returned at its shutdown check then no term logic ran and the term stays put, while a response plus a term movement would mean the handler ran normally and the suspicion is defeated. I registered the question as a gap on the same investigation rather than opening a new one, since it is the same handler and the same responsibility, and I assert nothing about the outcome until the receipt exists. The harness file was rewritten for this case and validates; the earlier harnesses are retained in their fixed experiments, and the four witnessed findings plus the unresolved threading claim remain recorded and unaffected.

investigations.question: For a running cluster, does the public configuration API expose the index of the latest configuration entry, and what value does a caller actually receive from ConfigurationFuture.Index()?

investigations.question: When authority over a node is lost by Shutdown() rather than by stepping down, does an already-accepted Apply/Barrier duty (a logFuture sitting in the buffered applyCh) still have a completion path?
investigations.hypothesis: Apply and Barrier hand the caller a logFuture as soon as the send into applyCh succeeds; with BatchApplyCh the channel is buffered, so acceptance and consumption are separate events. That logFuture has no ShutdownCh, Shutdown() closes shutdownCh and sets state Shutdown without draining applyCh, and both the main loop and runFSM leave on shutdownCh, so a future left in the buffer has no producer that can respond it: Error() blocks indefinitely and the caller's timeout, which only guarded the enqueue, cannot save it. runLeader's defer responds only futures on leaderState.inflight, so it does not cover a future that was never dispatched. Confirmed by observation: accepted in state Leader, still queued and unresponded after state Shutdown.
investigations.discriminator: Occupy the main loop inside a handler (a public Restore with a caller-supplied reader that stalls on its first Read, which is the handshake), accept one Barrier future through the ordinary public path so it lands in the buffered applyCh, then call Shutdown() and observe whether the future is ever responded: a completion would defeat the suspicion and must name the responding producer, while non-completion together with the future still being queued in applyCh shows the duty was accepted and then lost. Executed: no completion; the duty stayed queued with the node in state Shutdown.

knowledge.assertion: the caller's timeout guards only the enqueue, and the returned logFuture has no ShutdownCh, so completion is unbounded once the duty is accepted
Shutdown() drains nothing and runLeader's defer covers only leaderState.inflight, so a duty left in applyCh loses its producer

investigations.question: When a caller names a server that holds no vote as the target of an explicit leadership transfer, does the named server acquire leadership, and what happens to the sitting leader's authority?
investigations.hypothesis: LeadershipTransferToServer forwards the caller's id and address to the transfer routine, which only requires a replication state for that server, so a vote-less member is accepted as a target. On that target the TimeoutNow handler sets Candidate and the leadership-transfer flag unconditionally and the candidate loop skips pre-vote because of that flag, so the target runs a real election at term+1; but electSelf casts a self-vote only when the local server is a Voter in the latest configuration, and voters receiving a RequestVote from a member that holds no vote reject it - after already adopting the higher term. The requested transfer is therefore unachievable: the named target can never win, while its higher-term vote request deposes the sitting leader, and the caller's future is answered without error because losing leadership during a transfer is reported as success. Observed twice, on separate clusters with the same harness: target_ever_leader=false, transfer_err empty, term 2 to 4, original leader back in Leader state, and in both runs the target's term-3 campaign skipped pre-vote while the recovery election at term 4 ran one.
investigations.discriminator: Demote one real follower to a non-voter through the public API, then call LeadershipTransferToServer on that member and sample the real nodes for a bounded interval: whether the named target ever reaches Leader, which servers do lead, whether the original leader still leads at the end, the reported transfer error, and the term before and after. Executed twice with identical operands (CheckRuns 2b61659461634c04b53ec61c35541227 and cfde738278f04108b377b912cb3eb339); the control with a voter target (7224dba1ed234879b0cb1c65e5161bf7) moved leadership to the named server with a single term step.

investigations.question: Does the documented staging phase of AddVoter exist in the implementation: can a server added through the public AddVoter API be a Nonvoter or Staging member that the leader later promotes once it has caught up?
investigations.hypothesis: The public documentation for AddVoter states that the server is added as a staging server and that the leader promotes it to a voter once it is ready, and the membership design notes list catching new servers up before granting them a vote as a main goal. The implementation does not have that phase: nextConfiguration builds the AddVoter entry with Suffrage Voter outright, the separate Staging suffrage is only reachable by an explicit Promote command, and the library's own command documentation says AddStaging was actually AddVoter and is deprecated in its favour. The in-tree unit expectations agree with the implementation, expecting a Voter for a member added through AddVoter from missing, Staging or Nonvoter states, so the state the documentation describes is never entered through the public API and the promotion duty it describes is owed by nobody.
investigations.discriminator: Trace every producer of a configuration entry for AddVoter and every consumer of the Staging suffrage: if the only public path that can add a member writes Suffrage Voter and nothing in the non-test code ever issues Promote, the documented staging phase and its promotion duty do not exist, and the mismatch is decidable by reading rather than by execution. Executed by reading: the AddVoter case writes Voter, Promote is only reached by an explicit Promote command that no non-test caller issues, and the unit expectations for AddVoter match the AddStaging cases. An end-to-end witness is queued to confirm the consequence that the added member votes immediately.

investigations.question: Does the transport heartbeat fast path run appendEntries outside the main thread, and can that be observed as a term or leader-state change while the main loop is provably occupied?
investigations.hypothesis: raft.go marks processHeartbeat and appendEntries as main-thread-only, yet api.go installs processHeartbeat as the transport's heartbeat handler; the network transport classifies a strictly empty AppendEntries request (no previous entry, no entries, no leader commit index) as a heartbeat and dispatches it from its connection goroutine. That request still runs appendEntries' term logic before anything about entries matters, so an empty heartbeat carrying a term above the node's current term calls setState(Follower) and setCurrentTerm from that goroutine, mutating state the rest of the package treats as owned by the main thread. The in-memory transport used by the test facility explicitly does not support the handler, so the path is unreachable in the harness shapes used so far; a wrapper transport that installs the handler and fast-paths empty heartbeats the way the network transport does removes that obstacle without touching production code.
investigations.discriminator: Use a transport that implements the fast path the way the network transport does - forwarding strictly empty AppendEntries requests to the installed handler on the caller's goroutine - occupy the main loop deterministically with the already-validated Restore stall handshake, then deliver one empty heartbeat whose term is above the node's current term and read the node's term and leader state while the main loop is still inside its handler. A term or leader-state change observed inside that window witnesses off-main-thread mutation; no change, or a change only after the loop resumes, would defeat the suspicion. Queued for execution with exactly that harness.

scope.description: Read, from one running bootstrapped three-node cluster, the public configuration index (GetConfiguration().Index(), Stats()["latest_configuration_index"]) and the main-thread latestIndex/committedIndex of the same node, and emit them as one CA_EVENT JSON line.

scope.description: On one real bootstrapped cluster, accept a Barrier future while the main loop is occupied by a public Restore whose caller-supplied reader stalls, then call Shutdown() and emit one CA_EVENT JSON line recording whether the accepted future ever completed, how many duties remained queued in applyCh, the channel capacity, and the node state before acceptance and after shutdown.
assumptions: MakeCluster(3, conf) with conf.BatchApplyCh = true is a supported public configuration; BatchApplyCh buffers applyCh to MaxAppendEntries (config.go:169-174), which is what allows acceptance without a consumer.

Occupying the main loop with Restore and a reader that blocks on its first Read models a caller-supplied backup stream that stalls; the reader's first Read is the handshake proving the loop is inside that handler and can no longer select on applyCh.

basis.prefix: The harness (draft/assurance_generated_test.go) is one TestAssurance-prefixed test in the captured package. Then it occupies the main loop through the public API by calling leader.Restore(&SnapshotMeta{Version:1, Index:1, Term:1, Size:1}, reader, 0) in a goroutine, where reader is a caller-supplied io.Reader whose first Read closes a started channel and then blocks until released; receiving on started is the freeze handshake. Finally it releases the reader, records the error the Restore call returns once the handler resumes, and prints one CA_EVENT JSON line with all of these operands, so the decisive facts are the completion result, the queue depth, and the two node states observed on one instance in one execution.

scope.description: On one real four-node cluster, demote one follower to a non-voter through the public API, name it as the target of an explicit leadership transfer, and emit one CA_EVENT JSON line recording the reported transfer error, whether the named target ever reached Leader, which servers led during a bounded interval, the state of the original leader and of the target at the end, and the cluster term before and after.
assumptions: MakeCluster(4, t, nil) gives four real voters and a real leader; DemoteVoter is supported at protocol version 3, so the target stays a connected, log-receiving member of the committed configuration that simply holds no vote.
The target is chosen among nodes actually in Follower state, so it is a viable replication peer and the transfer routine's catch-up wait can be satisfied and the TimeoutNow actually delivered.
The bounded 3 s sampling window only observes leadership outcomes; the claim that a vote-less member cannot win rests on the election code (self-vote and voter gate), not on the window length.

basis.prefix: The harness (draft/assurance_generated_test.go) is one TestAssurance-prefixed test in the captured package, identical to the vote-less-target case except that the target is never demoted. It bootstraps a real four-voter cluster with MakeCluster(4, t, nil), takes the single elected leader via c.Leader(), waits for a follower using c.WaitEvent and c.GetInState, confirms from the leader's latest configuration that the target's suffrage is Voter, samples the maximum current term across c.rafts, calls leader.LeadershipTransferToServer(target.localID, target.localAddr) through the public API and records the error its future reports, then polls every 20 ms for up to 3 s across all nodes in c.rafts recording every address observed in Leader state, whether the named target was ever among them, and whether the original leader led again. It finishes by recording the maximum term after the window and the end states of the original leader and the target, and prints one CA_EVENT line tagged transfer_to_voter so the control event is distinguishable from the vote-less-target event in the same investigation.

scope.description: End-to-end witness on one real cluster: join a fresh, empty node through the public AddVoter API, record the suffrage the leader wrote for that member and the suffrage the new node itself sees, then take one original voter away and record whether a new command still commits - which it can only if the freshly added member counts as a voter.
assumptions: MakeCluster(2) plus MakeClusterNoBootstrap(1) merged and fully connected is the in-tree way to join a fresh node (raft_test.go:258-279), and the join itself is the public AddVoter call made by the elected leader.

Disconnecting one original voter is the discriminator: with three voters and one disconnected, a majority needs exactly the remaining original voter plus the new member, so a commit is only reachable if the new member votes; if the new member were the non-voting member the documentation describes, no majority would be reachable.
The apply future is waited on under a bounded interval because the completion of an accepted apply is not bounded by the caller's timeout.

basis.prefix: The harness (draft/assurance_generated_test.go) is one TestAssurance-prefixed test in the captured package. It bootstraps a real two-node cluster with MakeCluster(2, t, nil) and keeps a copy of the original members, creates a fresh single-node cluster with MakeClusterNoBootstrap(1, t, nil), merges the two clusters and fully connects them, then takes the elected leader with c.Leader() and the fresh node as the join target, identifying the other original voter as the peer to remove later. The join is the public leader.AddVoter(newNode.localID, newNode.localAddr, 0, 5s); its future is waited on under a bounded interval, recording add_err and, when it returned, the entry index it reports. The test then records the suffrage of the new member in the leader's latest configuration and in the new node's own latest configuration, and counts the voters in that configuration. It calls c.Disconnect on the other original voter's address and then applies one command through the public API, waiting on the apply future under a bounded interval and recording apply_with_one_original_voter_gone as committed, an error, or no_completion. Finally it records the new node's last index, the leader's state, and prints one CA_EVENT JSON line with all of these operands, so the decisive facts (the suffrage written for the added member, and whether a command can still commit with one original voter gone) come from the same cluster in one execution.

scope.description: Control for the AddVoter suffrage witness on the same cluster shape: join a fresh, empty node with the public AddNonvoter call instead, record the suffrage the leader wrote for it and the voter count, then disconnect one original voter and record whether a command still commits - which it should not, because a majority of the remaining voters is unreachable.
assumptions: MakeCluster(2) merged with MakeClusterNoBootstrap(1) and fully connected is the same join path the AddVoter witness used, so the only difference between the two executions is the public call that adds the node.
AddNonvoter is a supported public call at protocol version 3 and yields a member that receives log entries but holds no vote.

With one of the two original voters disconnected and the added member holding no vote, no majority of voters is reachable, so the command must not commit; a commit here would falsify the disconnect discriminator used by the witness.

basis.prefix: The harness (draft/assurance_generated_test.go) is one TestAssurance-prefixed control test in the captured package, identical to the AddVoter witness except for the join call. It bootstraps a real two-node cluster with MakeCluster(2, t, nil) and keeps a copy of the original members, creates a fresh single-node cluster with MakeClusterNoBootstrap(1, t, nil), merges and fully connects them, takes the elected leader and the fresh node, and identifies the other original voter. The join is the public leader.AddNonvoter(newNode.localID, newNode.localAddr, 0, 5s), waited on under a bounded interval, recording add_err and the entry index. The test records the suffrage of the new member in the leader's latest configuration and the number of voters there, calls c.Disconnect on the other original voter's address, then applies one command through the public API and waits on its future under a bounded interval, recording addnonvoter_suffrage with the apply result, the waited interval, the new node's last index and the leader's state, so the control's decisive operands (suffrage, voter count, and whether the command can still commit) come from the same cluster in one execution.

scope.description: On one real single-node Raft instance built over a transport that implements the heartbeat fast path, occupy the main loop inside a handler, deliver one empty heartbeat with a term above the node's current term, and emit one CA_EVENT JSON line recording the term and leader state sampled while the loop is still blocked, together with the heartbeat response and the states after the loop resumes.
assumptions: The wrapper transport reproduces the network transport's classification and dispatch faithfully (term set, leader address present, zero previous entry and term, no entries, zero leader commit index) and installs the handler exactly as NewRaft expects, so the handler under test is the production processHeartbeat and the appendEntries it calls.

The freeze handshake used here is the one already validated elsewhere in this run: the caller-supplied reader's first Read proves the main loop is inside its handler, so any term or state read before releasing it cannot have been produced by the main loop.
One node bootstrapped as the only voter becomes leader on its own, so no peer traffic interferes with the sample.
A term and state change in that window is a behaviour of the fast path; whether it has a harmful consequence is a separate question, and this execution does not claim one.

basis.prefix: The harness (draft/assurance_generated_test.go) is one TestAssurance-prefixed test in the captured package plus two helper types it defines locally. It creates a real in-memory transport, wraps it in fastPathTransport, sets the config's LocalID to that address, bootstraps a single-voter configuration with BootstrapCluster and starts the node with NewRaft using an in-memory store, snapshot store and MockFSM, then waits (bounded) for the node to reach Leader state. It occupies the main loop by calling the public Restore with a caller-supplied reader whose first Read closes a channel and then blocks; receiving on that channel is the freeze handshake. While the loop is blocked it samples the node's term and state, builds an empty AppendEntriesRequest with a leader address and a term one above the current term, and delivers it through fastPathTransport.deliverHeartbeat, which applies the network transport's classification and invokes the installed handler on this goroutine, recording the returned success flag or error. It then samples the term and state again while the loop is still blocked, releases the reader so the occupied handler can return, records the Restore error and the states after release, prints one CA_EVENT JSON line with all operands, and shuts the node down.

scope.description: On one real single-node Raft instance built over a transport that implements the heartbeat fast path, deliver one empty heartbeat while the node is live as a control, then shut the node down while leaving its transport open and deliver a second empty heartbeat, emitting one CA_EVENT JSON line that records whether each delivery got a response, how long the second waited, and the node's term and state around each.
assumptions: The wrapper transport reproduces the network transport's classification, synchronous dispatch to the installed handler and response wait faithfully, so the handler under test is the production processHeartbeat and the appendEntries it calls.

Calling Shutdown() without waiting on the returned future leaves the in-memory transport open, which is the state a caller creates when it does not wait, and the transport is only closed when the shutdown future is waited on at the end of the test.

The second heartbeat carries a term one above the node's current term, so if the handler ran its term logic the term would move and be observable; a term that stays put together with no response is evidence the handler returned at its shutdown check.

A bounded response wait is the only practical way to observe a missing response in-process; the zero-response reading is interpreted together with the source fact that the handler has no other response path once the shutdown channel is closed.

basis.prefix: The harness (draft/assurance_generated_test.go) is one TestAssurance-prefixed test in the captured package plus a local transport wrapper. It creates a real in-memory transport, wraps it in a type that stores the handler set by NewRaft and dispatches strictly empty AppendEntries requests to it on the caller's goroutine before waiting on the supplied response channel, bootstraps a single-voter configuration with BootstrapCluster and starts the node with NewRaft over in-memory stores, snapshots and MockFSM, then waits (bounded) for Leader state. It records the term, delivers an empty heartbeat one term above it through the wrapper's fast path with a bounded wait and records the control outcome, term and state. It then calls Shutdown() and deliberately does not wait on the returned future, sleeps briefly so the node's routines observe the shutdown, records the term and state, and delivers a second empty heartbeat one term above the current one with a bounded wait, recording whether a response arrived, how long the wait was and whether the term moved. It prints one CA_EVENT JSON line with all of these operands and only then waits on the shutdown future, which is what closes the transport.
